claim: The Golgi complex in mammalian cells plays a crucial role in membrane trafficking and post-translational modification of proteins and lipids.
source: The Golgi complex in mammalian cells plays a crucial role in membrane trafficking and post-translational modification of proteins and lipids (cargos).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The Golgi complex is centrally positioned around the microtubule organization center.
source: Centrally positioned around the microtubule organization center (Glick and Luini, 2011; Klumperman, 2011), it comprises laterally connected Golgi stacks, each containing 4–7 tightly adjacent membrane sacs known as cisternae.
evidence: Supported by citations to Glick and Luini, 2011 and Klumperman, 2011.

claim: A Golgi stack comprises laterally connected Golgi stacks, each containing 4–7 tightly adjacent membrane sacs known as cisternae.
source: Centrally positioned around the microtubule organization center (Glick and Luini, 2011; Klumperman, 2011), it comprises laterally connected Golgi stacks, each containing 4–7 tightly adjacent membrane sacs known as cisternae.
evidence: Supported by citations to Glick and Luini, 2011 and Klumperman, 2011.

claim: A Golgi stack is conventionally recognized to have three regions: the cis, medial, and trans-Golgi.
source: Conventionally, a Golgi stack is recognized to have three regions: the cis, medial, and trans-Golgi.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The trans-Golgi network (TGN) assembles outside the trans-side of a Golgi stack and is mainly composed of tubular and vesicular membranes.
source: The trans-Golgi network (TGN) assembles outside the trans-side of a Golgi stack and is mainly composed of tubular and vesicular membranes (De Matteis and Luini, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Matteis and Luini, 2008.

claim: In the secretory pathway, newly synthesized cargos exit the ER at the ER exit site (ERES), pass the ER and Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC), and reach the Golgi.
source: In the secretory pathway, newly synthesized cargos exit the ER at the ER exit site (ERES), pass the ER and Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC), and reach the Golgi.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the secretory pathway.

claim: Cargos transit from the cis-side through the medial and eventually reach the trans-side of the Golgi, where they exit the Golgi and target the plasma membrane.
source: Cargos subsequently transit from the cis-side through the medial and eventually reach the trans-side of the Golgi, where they exit the Golgi and target the plasma membrane (Bergmann and Singer, 1983; Castle et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergmann and Singer, 1983 and Castle et al., 1972.

claim: The mechanism of intra-Golgi transport of secretory cargos remains enigmatic.
source: Despite decades of research, the Golgi remains one of the most enigmatic organelles, particularly regarding the mechanism of intra-Golgi transport of secretory cargos (Emr et al., 2009; Glick and Luini, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Emr et al., 2009 and Glick and Luini, 2011.

claim: In the classic cisternal progression model, secretory cargos passively reside within Golgi cisternae, which progress or mature from the cis to the trans-Golgi cisternae.
source: In the classic cisternal progression or maturation model, secretory cargos passively reside within Golgi cisternae, which progress or mature from the cis to the trans-Golgi cisternae to facilitate the forward or anterograde transport of cargos.
evidence: This describes the classic cisternal progression model.

claim: The classic cisternal progression model predicts that all secretory cargos should have the same and constant intra-Golgi transport and Golgi exit velocity.
source: The model predicts that all secretory cargos should have the same and constant intra-Golgi transport and Golgi exit velocity.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the cisternal progression model.

claim: The cisternal progression model can provide a plausible explanation for the intra-Golgi transition of oversized secretory cargos, such as procollagen I.
source: It can provide a plausible explanation for the intra-Golgi transition of oversized secretory cargos, such as procollagen I (Bonfanti et al., 1998; Mironov et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonfanti et al., 1998 and Mironov et al., 2001.

claim: Direct observations of cisternal maturation have been made in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Moreover, direct observations of cisternal maturation have been made in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Kurokawa et al., 2019; Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006), although similar observations have not been reported in mammalian cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kurokawa et al., 2019; Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006.

claim: Similar observations of cisternal maturation have not been reported in mammalian cells.
source: Moreover, direct observations of cisternal maturation have been made in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Kurokawa et al., 2019; Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006), although similar observations have not been reported in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the absence of observations in mammalian cells.

claim: The budding yeast Golgi differs significantly from the mammalian one in the cisternal organization – it scatters throughout the cytoplasm as unstacked compartments.
source: However, the budding yeast Golgi differs significantly from the mammalian one in the cisternal organization – it scatters throughout the cytoplasm as unstacked compartments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural differences between yeast and mammalian Golgi.

claim: In the stable compartment model, Golgi cisternae are stable entities.
source: In contrast, the stable compartment model posits that Golgi cisternae are stable entities.
evidence: This describes the stable compartment model.

claim: In the stable compartment model, carriers actively move secretory cargos from one cisterna or compartment to the next, from the cis to the trans-side.
source: During intra-Golgi transport, carriers actively move secretory cargos from one cisterna or compartment to the next, from the cis to the trans-side, while post-translational modification enzymes remain stationary.
evidence: This describes the stable compartment model.

claim: In the stable compartment model, different cargos can exhibit distinct intra-Golgi transport and Golgi exit velocities.
source: As a result, different cargos can exhibit distinct intra-Golgi transport and Golgi exit velocities under this model.
evidence: This is a prediction of the stable compartment model.

claim: The rim progression model is a modified version of the stable compartment model.
source: To account for the intra-Golgi transport of oversized secretory cargos, such as procollagen I, a modified version of the stable compartment model, the rim progression model, has been proposed (Lavieu et al., 2013; Pfeffer, 2010; Volchuk et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lavieu et al., 2013; Pfeffer, 2010; Volchuk et al., 2000.

claim: In the rim progression model, each Golgi cisterna has a stable interior domain and a dynamic rim domain.
source: In this model, each Golgi cisterna seems to have a stable interior domain and a dynamic rim domain; the rim domain of Golgi cisternae undergoes constant en bloc fission and fusion, carrying small or large cargos to the next cisternae for intra-Golgi cargo transport.
evidence: This describes the rim progression model.

claim: The rim partitioning of large secretory cargos is supported by previous EM studies of procollagen I.
source: The rim partitioning of large secretory cargos is supported by previous EM studies of procollagen I (Bonfanti et al., 1998), FM4 aggregates (Lavieu et al., 2013), and algal protein aggregates (Engel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonfanti et al., 1998; Lavieu et al., 2013; Engel et al., 2015.

claim: During their intra-Golgi transition, small cargos, such as CD59, E-cadherin, and VSVG, localize to the cisternal interior, coinciding with Golgi glycosyltransferases.
source: Furthermore, we have recently demonstrated in fluorescence microscopy that during their intra-Golgi transition, small cargos, such as CD59, E-cadherin, and VSVG, localize to the cisternal interior, coinciding with Golgi glycosyltransferases, while large cargos, such as FM4 aggregates and collagenX, position themselves at the cisternal rim, where trafficking machinery components localize (Tie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tie et al., 2018.

claim: Large cargos, such as FM4 aggregates and collagenX, position themselves at the cisternal rim, where trafficking machinery components localize.
source: Furthermore, we have recently demonstrated in fluorescence microscopy that during their intra-Golgi transition, small cargos, such as CD59, E-cadherin, and VSVG, localize to the cisternal interior, coinciding with Golgi glycosyltransferases, while large cargos, such as FM4 aggregates and collagenX, position themselves at the cisternal rim, where trafficking machinery components localize (Tie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tie et al., 2018.

claim: The classic cisternal progression model posits that secretory cargos linearly depart the trans-Golgi.
source: The classic cisternal progression model posits that secretory cargos linearly depart the trans-Golgi.
evidence: This is a prediction of the cisternal progression model.

claim: Cargo exit kinetics have been shown to adhere to a first-order exponential relationship rather than a linear one.
source: Contrary to this, cargo exit kinetics have been shown to adhere to a first-order exponential relationship rather than a linear one (Hirschberg et al., 1998; Patterson et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hirschberg et al., 1998; Patterson et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2020.

claim: The rapid partitioning model suggests that cargos rapidly diffuse throughout the Golgi stack, segregating into multiple post-translational processing and export domains.
source: This model suggests that cargos rapidly diffuse throughout the Golgi stack, segregating into multiple post-translational processing and export domains, where cargos are packed into carriers bound for the plasma membrane.
evidence: This describes the rapid partitioning model introduced by Patterson et al., 2008.

claim: Synchronized traffic waves have been observed through various techniques, including electron microscopy (EM) and advanced light microscopy methods.
source: Nonetheless, synchronized traffic waves have been observed through various techniques, including electron microscopy (EM) (Trucco et al., 2004) and advanced light microscopy methods we developed, such as GLIM and side-averaging (Tie et al., 2016; Tie et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trucco et al., 2004; Tie et al., 2016; Tie et al., 2022.

claim: Ministacks obtained under prolonged nocodazole treatment (≥3 hr) largely represent the native Golgi stack.
source: Extensive studies have provided strong evidence that ministacks obtained under prolonged nocodazole treatment (≥3 hr), the condition employed in our studies, largely represent the native Golgi stack (Cole et al., 1996; Fourriere et al., 2016; Rogalski et al., 1984; Schueder et al., 2024; Tie et al., 2018; Trucco et al., 2004; Van De Moortele et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: GLIM can precisely pinpoint a Golgi protein's cisternal localization with nanometer accuracy in Golgi ministacks.
source: We developed a numerical Golgi localization tool called Golgi localization by imaging centers of mass (GLIM) that can precisely pinpoint a Golgi protein's cisternal localization with nanometer accuracy in Golgi ministacks (Tie et al., 2017; Tie et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tie et al., 2017; Tie et al., 2016.

claim: The intra-Golgi transport velocity of a secretory cargo decreases during their transition from the cis to the trans-side of the Golgi.
source: Leveraging our recently developed Golgi imaging tools in nocodazole-induced Golgi ministacks, we found that the intra-Golgi transport velocity of a secretory cargo decreases during their transition from the cis to the trans-side of the Golgi, and different cargos exhibit distinct velocities even within the same cisternae.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Different cargos exhibit distinct velocities even within the same cisternae.
source: Leveraging our recently developed Golgi imaging tools in nocodazole-induced Golgi ministacks, we found that the intra-Golgi transport velocity of a secretory cargo decreases during their transition from the cis to the trans-side of the Golgi, and different cargos exhibit distinct velocities even within the same cisternae.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: There is a vast variation in the Golgi residence times of different cargos.
source: We observed a vast variation in the Golgi residence times of different cargos.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Truncation of the luminal domain causes the Golgi residence time of Tac to extend from 16 min to 3.4 hr.
source: Remarkably, truncation of the luminal domain causes the Golgi residence time of Tac — a standard transmembrane secretory cargo without intra-Golgi recycling signals — to extend from 16 min to a notable 3.4 hr.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: When COPI-mediated intra-Golgi retrograde transport was inhibited by brefeldin A, nocodazole-induced Golgi can remain stacked for over 30–60 min.
source: Additionally, when COPI-mediated intra-Golgi retrograde transport was inhibited by brefeldin A, we found that nocodazole-induced Golgi can remain stacked for over 30–60 min.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The findings challenge the classical cisternal progression model and suggest the stable compartment nature of the Golgi.
source: Therefore, our findings challenge the classical cisternal progression model and suggest the stable compartment nature of the Golgi.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: All LQ vs. t plots fit the first-order exponential function well with an adjusted R2 (adj. R2)≥0.85.
source: As previously reported, all LQ vs. t plots fit the following first-order exponential function (Equation 1) well with an adjusted R2 (adj. R2)≥0.85 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-T, left panels).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dLQ/dt of all RUSH reporters slows to zero as they transit across the Golgi stack to reach LQ = y0 at the trans-Golgi or TGN.
source: It is evident that the dLQ/dt of all our RUSH reporters slows to zero as they transit across the Golgi stack to reach LQ = y0 at the trans-Golgi or TGN (Figure 2A-J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-T, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intra-Golgi transport velocity of a secretory cargo does not remain constant, contradicting the prediction of the classic cisternal progression model.
source: Hence, the intra-Golgi transport velocity of a secretory cargo does not remain constant, contradicting the prediction of the classic cisternal progression model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing variable transport velocities.

claim: CollagenX has been known to assemble into oligomers.
source: CollagenX has been known to assemble into oligomers (Kwan et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwan et al., 1991.

claim: SBP-GFP-collagenX forms large aggregates containing ~190 copies.
source: We previously reported that the collagenX RUSH reporter, SBP-GFP-collagenX, forms large aggregates containing ~190 copies (Tie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tie et al., 2018.

claim: SBP-GFP-collagenX aggregates have an estimated mean size of ~40 nm.
source: With an estimated mean size of ~40 nm, these aggregates are much smaller than FM4 aggregates and procollagen I (>300 nm) (Bonfanti et al., 1998; Volchuk et al., 2000) and, therefore, are not excluded from conventional transport vesicles, which typically have a size of 50–100 nm.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the size of the aggregates.

claim: Conventional transport vesicles typically have a size of 50–100 nm.
source: With an estimated mean size of ~40 nm, these aggregates are much smaller than FM4 aggregates and procollagen I (>300 nm) (Bonfanti et al., 1998; Volchuk et al., 2000) and, therefore, are not excluded from conventional transport vesicles, which typically have a size of 50–100 nm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vesicle sizes.

claim: While conventional secretory cargos partition to the cisternal interior during intra-Golgi transport, large cargos such as FM4 aggregates and collagenX preferentially localize to the cisternal rim.
source: However, our previous findings showed that while conventional secretory cargos partition to the cisternal interior during intra-Golgi transport, large cargos such as FM4 aggregates and collagenX preferentially localize to the cisternal rim (Tie et al., 2018), highlighting distinct intra-Golgi transport behavior for different cargo sizes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tie et al., 2018.

claim: The intra-Golgi transport of SBP-GFP-collagenX followed a first-order exponential function, with a tintra of 8±1 (mean ± SD, n=3).
source: Using the RUSH assay, our LQ vs. t data demonstrated that the intra-Golgi transport of SBP-GFP-collagenX followed a first-order exponential function, with a tintra of 8±1 (mean ± SD, n=3) (Figure 3A–C; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A–C and Table 1.

claim: SBP-GFP-collagenX exited at the trans-Golgi, with a y0 of 0.92±0.08 (mean ± SD, n=3).
source: SBP-GFP-collagenX exited at the trans-Golgi, with a y0 of 0.92±0.08 (mean ± SD, n=3).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data.

claim: The instantaneous intra-Golgi transport velocity (dLQ/dt) of SBP-GFP-collagenX decreases in accordance with a first-order exponential function.
source: Additionally, the instantaneous intra-Golgi transport velocity (dLQ/dt) of SBP-GFP-collagenX also decreases in accordance with a first-order exponential function (Figure 3A–C; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A–C and Table 1.

claim: When passing through the medial and trans-Golgi regions at t=10 and 20 min after biotin chase, SBP-GFP-collagenX appeared as double puncta, supporting its cisternal rim localization.
source: When passing through the medial and trans-Golgi regions at t=10 and 20 min after biotin chase, SBP-GFP-collagenX appeared as double puncta, supporting its cisternal rim localization (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 40 min after biotin chase, numerous SBP-GFP-collagenX-positive carriers were observed surrounding the trans-Golgi, indicating a process of Golgi exiting.
source: 40 min after biotin chase, numerous SBP-GFP-collagenX-positive carriers were observed surrounding the trans-Golgi, indicating a process of Golgi exiting (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cisternal rim partitioned large-sized secretory cargos might follow intra-Golgi transport kinetics similar to those of cisternal interior partitioned conventional secretory cargos.
source: In summary, our findings demonstrated that cisternal rim partitioned large-sized secretory cargos might follow intra-Golgi transport kinetics similar to those of cisternal interior partitioned conventional secretory cargos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on collagenX.

claim: One LQ unit corresponds to 274 nm.
source: In our previous work, through side-averaging, we determined that one LQ unit corresponds to 274 nm (Tie et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tie et al., 2022.

claim: Different secretory cargos exhibit varied transport velocities even within the same cisternae or at the same LQ values.
source: When plotting the instantaneous intra-Golgi transport velocity (nm/min) against the LQ for selected RUSH reporters, as seen in Figure 4A, we observed that different secretory cargos exhibit varied transport velocities even within the same cisternae or at the same LQ values.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At LQ = 0.40, the instantaneous intra-Golgi transport velocities of SBP-GFP, SBP-GFP-Tac-TC, SBP-GFP-CD59, SBP-GFP-Tac, and TNFα-SBP-GFP are 6.1, 8.0, 9.2, 14.6, and 20.5 nm/min, respectively.

claim: Different secretory cargos possess distinct intra-Golgi transport velocities within the same Golgi cisternae, challenging the prediction made by the classic cisternal progression model.
source: These findings highlighted that different secretory cargos possess distinct intra-Golgi transport velocities within the same Golgi cisternae, challenging the prediction made by the classic cisternal progression model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Studies have demonstrated that cargos exit the Golgi by following the first-order exponential kinetics.
source: However, studies have demonstrated that cargos exit the Golgi by following the first-order exponential kinetics (Hirschberg et al., 1998; Patterson et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hirschberg et al., 1998; Patterson et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2020.

claim: The Golgi residence time is a cargo's duration at the trans-Golgi cisternae before exit and is a metric for Golgi retention.
source: The Golgi residence time is a cargo's duration at the trans-Golgi cisternae before exit and is a metric for Golgi retention (Sun et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020.

claim: Golgi residence times of secretory cargos display a wide range of values.
source: Our extensive measurement demonstrated that Golgi residence times of secretory cargos display a wide range of values (Table 2).

claim: TNFα-SBP-GFP has a Golgi residence time of 6.0±0.4 min (mean ± SEM, n=73).

evidence: Supported by citations to Gut et al., 1998; Sun et al., 2020.

source: Their Golgi residence time was documented at 16±2 min (mean ± SEM, n=45) and 7.8±0.7 min (mean ± SEM, n=26), respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 2.

claim: GFP-CD8a has a Golgi residence time of 7.8±0.7 min (mean ± SEM, n=26).
source: Their Golgi residence time was documented at 16±2 min (mean ± SEM, n=45) and 7.8±0.7 min (mean ± SEM, n=26), respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 2.

claim: GFP-CD8a-TC has an LQ of 0.86±0.05 (mean ± SEM, n=76).
source: Second, their LQs, 0.94±0.02 (mean ± SEM, n=118) and 0.86±0.05 (mean ± SEM, n=76), combined with their cisternal interior localization (Figure 5B; Sun et al., 2020), indicate that they primarily reside within the interior of the trans-cisternae, similar to many Golgi glycosyltransferases (Tie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data.

claim: GFP-Tac-TC and GFP-CD8a-TC primarily reside within the interior of the trans-cisternae, similar to many Golgi glycosyltransferases.

claim: GFP-Tac-TC's LQ (0.94) is close to its Golgi exit site, y0 (0.95–1.16).
source: Considering that GFP-Tac-TC's LQ (0.94) is close to its Golgi exit site, y0 (0.95–1.16) (Table 1; Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1M-O), measured by its RUSH version, there are two possible retrieval pathways, acting at either post-Golgi or intra-Golgi stages.

claim: VHH-anti-GFP-mCherry localized to the Golgi in a significant fraction of MGAT2-GFP-expressing cells (32%, n=266) but not in MGAT1-GFP cells (0%, n=102) after 8 hr of continuous internalization.
source: We found that VHH-anti-GFP-mCherry localized to the Golgi in a significant fraction of MGAT2-GFP-expressing cells (32%, n=266) but not in MGAT1-GFP cells (0%, n=102) after 8 hr of continuous internalization (Figure 5C).

claim: MGAT2, but not MGAT1, has a Golgi retrieval mechanism.
source: This result is consistent with our previous report that MGAT2, but not MGAT1, has a Golgi retrieval mechanism (Sun et al., 2021), although its molecular mechanism is still unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: VHH-anti-GFP-mCherry did not localize to the Golgi in cells expressing GFP-Tac-TC, suggesting that GFP-Tac-TC might not possess a post-Golgi retrieval mechanism targeting the Golgi.

claim: GFP-Tac and GFP-Tac-TC share identical TMD and cytosolic tail sequences.
source: Since GFP-Tac and GFP-Tac-TC share identical TMD and cytosolic tail sequences, if such a retrograde mechanism existed, GFP-Tac would have a similar Golgi residence time to GFP-Tac-TC.

claim: GFP-Tac-TC and GFP-CD8a-TC might not have retrieval signals to facilitate their Golgi residence.
source: Therefore, we argue that GFP-Tac-TC and GFP-CD8a-TC might not have retrieval signals to facilitate their Golgi residence, although proving a protein does not possess a transport signal is challenging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and reasoning.

claim: The cisternal interior is continuous with the cisternal rim both in membrane and lumen.
source: Since the cisternal interior is continuous with the cisternal rim both in membrane and lumen, our findings suggest that the cisternal interior at the trans-Golgi might be a stable domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Golgi structure.

claim: The cisternal interior at the trans-Golgi might be a stable domain.
source: Since the cisternal interior is continuous with the cisternal rim both in membrane and lumen, our findings suggest that the cisternal interior at the trans-Golgi might be a stable domain.

claim: Retention within the trans-side stable domain, rather than continuous retrieval to counter the cisternal progression (treadmilling), could be the primary mechanism for the long Golgi residence times of GFP-Tac-TC and GFP-CD8a-TC.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: COPI functions in the retrograde direction at the ER-Golgi interface and within the Golgi.
source: COPI functions in the retrograde direction at the ER-Golgi interface and within the Golgi (Glick and Luini, 2011; Popoff et al., 2011; Rabouille and Klumperman, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glick and Luini, 2011; Popoff et al., 2011; Rabouille and Klumperman, 2005.

claim: According to the classic cisternal progression model, upon the compromise of COPI, intra-Golgi recycling would stop, and the Golgi stack would continuously lose its materials and eventually disappear.
source: According to the classic cisternal progression model, COPI-mediated retrograde intra-Golgi transport recycles resident transmembrane proteins, such as glycosyltransferases and transport machinery components. This model predicts that upon the compromise of COPI, intra-Golgi recycling would stop, and the Golgi stack would continuously lose its materials and eventually disappear, depending on the cisternal progression rate.
evidence: This is a prediction of the cisternal progression model.

claim: COPI has been documented to function in the anterograde ER-to-Golgi transport.
source: In addition to its retrograde role, COPI has also been documented to function in the anterograde ER-to-Golgi transport (Monetta et al., 2007; Weigel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Monetta et al., 2007; Weigel et al., 2021.

claim: BFA rapidly dissociates COPI and clathrin from the Golgi, inhibits the ER-to-Golgi trafficking, and causes the fusion of the Golgi with the ER in 10–20 min.
source: To test the role of COPI in the Golgi organization, we employed BFA, a small molecule fungal metabolite that rapidly dissociates COPI and clathrin from the Golgi, inhibits the ER-to-Golgi trafficking, and causes the fusion of the Golgi with the ER in 10–20 min (Klausner et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klausner et al., 1992.

claim: BFA rapidly inactivates class I ARFs, which recruit COPI and clathrin coats to the Golgi membrane.
source: It does so by rapidly inactivating class I ARFs, which recruit COPI and clathrin coats to the Golgi membrane (Donaldson et al., 1992; Helms and Rothman, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donaldson et al., 1992; Helms and Rothman, 1992.

claim: Nocodazole-induced Golgi ministacks are more resistant to BFA, and the disappearance of Golgi occurs at a much later time (>30 min).
source: In contrast to the native Golgi, nocodazole-induced Golgi ministacks have been documented to be more resistant to BFA, and, hence, the disappearance of Golgi occurs at a much later time (>30 min) (Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1990.

source: Strikingly, we observed that Golgi puncta are still stacked as all measured LQs exhibited a relative arrangement similar to those of the pre-BFA treatment (t=0 min) (Figure 6F).

claim: BFA treatment altered the physical dimensions of ministacks.

claim: The distance from GM130 to GalT-mCherry decreased from 300±10 nm (mean ± SEM, n=34) to 190±30 (mean ± SEM, n=13) after 30 min of BFA treatment, indicating axial shrinkage of ministacks.
source: We observed the distance from GM130 to GalT-mCherry, d(GM130-GalT-mCherry), decreased from 300±10 nm (mean ± SEM, n=34)–190±30 (mean ± SEM, n=13) after 30 min of BFA treatment, indicating axial shrinkage of ministacks (Figure 6G).

claim: LQs of all three TGN markers, TGN46, CD8a-furin, and CD8a-CI-M6PR, decreased and approached that of the trans-Golgi, suggesting a collapse of the TGN.
source: Furthermore, LQs of all three TGN markers, TGN46, CD8a-furin, and CD8a-CI-M6PR, decreased and approached that of the trans-Golgi, suggesting a collapse of the TGN (Figure 6F), possibly due to the dissociation of clathrin and its adaptor proteins.

claim: The collapse of the TGN was supported by the side-averaging images, in which CD8a-furin gradually approached the trans-Golgi labeled by GalT-mCherry over time.
source: This collapse of the TGN was further supported by the side-averaging images, in which CD8a-furin gradually approached the trans-Golgi labeled by GalT-mCherry over time (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6H.

evidence: This is supported by the experimental data.

claim: The Golgi maintains its stacked organization for at least 30–60 min, even in the absence of COPI-mediated intra-Golgi retrograde transport.
source: Despite dramatic changes in the TGN and shrinkage of the axial length of the Golgi minitack, our data demonstrate that the Golgi maintains its stacked organization for at least 30–60 min, even in the absence of COPI-mediated intra-Golgi retrograde transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The Golgi might not be a dynamic equilibrium between the cisternal progression and retrograde trafficking and argues for a by-default stable nature of the Golgi stack.
source: Our findings suggest that the Golgi might not be a dynamic equilibrium between the cisternal progression and retrograde trafficking and argue for a by-default stable nature of the Golgi stack.

claim: The findings support the rim progression model, a modified version of the stable compartment model.
source: Combined with our current observations of differential intra-Golgi transport velocities among distinct secretory cargos (Figures 2—4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the stable trans-Golgi interior localization of GFP-Tac-TC (Sun et al., 2020) and GFP-CD8a-TC (Figure 5B and Table 2), these findings support the modified version of the stable compartment model – the rim progression model (Lavieu et al., 2013; Pfeffer, 2010; Volchuk et al., 2000).
